newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's export targets too optimistic - minister.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's export targets too optimistic - minister.

text.p: Serbia will unlikely to be able to raise exports to 3.2 billion dollars and reduce the current trade gap to $500 million, two key trade targets for 1996, a senior government official said on Thursday.

"Official forecasts that the trade deficit would drop to only $500 million by the end of 1996 are too optimistic, but I wish your estimates were right," Djordje Siradovic, Yugoslav trade minister, told a gathering of Serbian businessmen.
Siradovic said the problem was not so much high imports but a lack of exports and insufficient supply of competitive goods.
"But more than that, it is a problem of overall economic policy and not just of the foreign trade sector," he said.
Latest figures released by the Serbian Chamber of Commerce show Serbia's January-August trade gap at $1.057 billion, with exports of $1.034 billion and imports of $2.091 billion.
Agriculture is the biggest export earner, with grain trade alone generating 12 percent of total export income.
Other top export-earning goods included raspberries, wood, pharmaceuticals, car tyres and copper products, the Chamber of Commerce said in its report.

The Yugoslav minister said U.N. sanctions imposed nearly four years ago to punish Belgrade for its support for Bosnian Serbs had merely worsened existing difficulties even before the trade embargo was imposed.
"We still have an export market, but it has changed. A huge Soviet market offering barter arrangements exists no longer."
According to Siradovic, barter arrangements, particularly with China, are needed.
"It is not easy to export from Serbia. But in turn, we get oil and raw materials to revive our production," he said.
The minister insisted Yugoslavia would not base its foreign trade on barter arrangements. He said the country needed some time to stabilise its export network.
He said the government had not paid enough attention to and fully analysed other export markets.

Siradovic said major domestic companies that once dominated foreign trade now faced great difficulties in kick-starting their production and promised the government would help them. He did not elaborate on his remarks. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
